summary.name: Why Percentiles Don't Work the Way You Think
summary.one_liner: A VividCortex blog post explaining why averaging percentile metrics (such as StatsD/Graphite upper_99) is mathematically flawed, and how banded metrics, histograms and heatmaps can give more accurate latency views.
use_cases: Deciding whether to store p99 metrics in a time series database
Understanding why averages hide outliers in monitoring
Designing banded or histogram-based latency metrics
Choosing between percentiles, histograms and heatmaps for latency dashboards
Evaluating StatsD percentile metrics in Graphite
summary.what_it_does: The post argues that percentiles cannot be correctly averaged or resampled, because computing them requires the original population of events, while time series databases typically store and average aggregated values over time. It reviews the problems with averages in monitoring and explains what a percentile represents. It describes alternatives: histograms, approximate sketches, and banded metrics that store counts per value range from which percentiles can be computed. It also covers heatmaps as a way to visualize full latency distributions. The author states that VividCortex's DPM does not currently store percentile metrics and plans to store banded metrics at one-second granularity, downsampled to one-minute histograms.
notable: Explains why averaging p99 values over time is mathematically meaningless
Covers banded metrics as a way to compute percentiles that survive resampling
Describes VividCortex DPM's planned per-second banded metrics and one-minute downsampling
References Graphite, StatsD, Circonus, and Phusion Passenger examples
caveats: The DPM histogram and percentile features were planned future work at the time of writing, with no release date promised
Banded metric approach depends on whether the time series database query language supports the needed calculations
Percentiles from stored or resampled metrics are approximations and can be misleading if misunderstood
